doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Son John Allred and his path from Disney to Woody Herman
summary: He recounts John moving to Orlando, getting a Disney job, advice to read well, and joining Woody Herman.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Do you guys ever — I can just picture this scenario where your son calls you up and says, “Hey guess what I’m doing?” And you say, “Oh yeah, well guess what I’m doing.” Like one upsmanship.

It is. There’s a little bit of that. Like I sat in with Woody’s band one time when they played at Disney here, and played a couple of tunes with them. But no John, I always — a favorite barb I always lay on the people, I say, “Yeah it’s a special thing when you have a son that plays the same instrument as you.” I said, “There’s a defining moment in your life when your son looks at you and says, ‘no dad, it goes like this.’” And I don’t know if that actually happened like that but it did you know, and he’d help me with some of this. Because he took my advice. John, you know him and his mother and I had divorced and so he lived with his mom up in North Carolina until he graduated from high school. So then John moved down to Orlando with me and my new wife and I said, “Well what do you want to do?” I said, “If you want to go to college I’ll be happy to help you as much as I can financially. If you want to go to the Navy I know most of the guys out at the base” because I’d played with the Navy unit band. I said, “What do you want to do?” He said, “I just want to play.” I said, “Well that’s easier said than done.” So I took him out to Disney and had him, set up an audition with a rhythm section and my son. Two or three of the guys were there when I auditioned you know, down in Miami. So John played about three tunes, and Sonny Anderson and another guy said, he says, “We’ll take him.” We’ll take him. I said, “What are you going to do.” He said, “Well it just so happens that we have a young Dixieland-type show band at Disneyland in Anaheim that the trombone player is leaving to go back to school, and if John wants the gig it’s his. John went from high school to work for Disney. And of course, and I always say this, he had a good job for about three years and pissed all the money away. He did buy a car, but he did hang around a lot of the rehearsal bands in LA, got to meet a lot of people, and he would go out and play these gigs, and I pushed him on. I said, “John, I don’t care what kind of gig or how stupid it might seem to you, it’s experience.” And I stressed the reading man. I said, “John,” I learned to read okay. I was never a great reader. But I said, “I pushed it aside because I started playing by ear so early in my career, before I was even in seventh grade, playing jam sessions.” So I said, “That’s paramount, man, you’ve got to read your ass off. Nothing that’s going to baffle you.” I says that will bring dividends because I can tell you’ve got a good ear, you can play jazz, and you couple that with being an excellent reader and I says you’ll never be out of work. And I was right.
Now he can do a Broadway show and —
